Additional evidence shows that clinician shift and context-of-use changes can meaningfully alter real-world behavior and system performance, reinforcing the need for ongoing surveillance rather than one-time validation [ 4 ].
AI should not be framed as a safeguard that replaces clinical reasoning, but as a tool that reshapes it.

unlisted_practices: Keep prescription verification an active cognitive process for clinicians even when AI systems offer reassurance.
Give medication safety leaders visibility into and authority over AI-enabled tools that influence prescribing decisions.
Clarify who is responsible for monitoring AI system behavior, how performance changes are detected, and when intervention is required.
Do not equate the absence of an AI alert with prescription correctness, and do not treat efficiency gains as evidence of safety.
Explicitly recognize professional risks to clinicians, such as erosion of verification skills, moral distress, and accountability ambiguity, when deploying AI verification.

screen.reason: This is an editorial providing commentary and governance recommendations on the deployment, monitoring, and socio-technical safety of AI-enabled prescription verification systems.
